The figure of 53 percent is the markup on cost, which uses cost as the denominator and is always larger. Mixing up margin and markup is a common pricing error that can badly understate the needed price.
questions.hint: Divide profit by the selling price, not by the cost.

questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: Demand for a life-saving medicine sold by Verdant Software, a startup firm in Valeview changes very little when the price rises. Which statement about elasticity is most accurate?
questions.explanation: When quantity barely responds to price, demand is inelastic, with an absolute elasticity below 1. In that case the percentage gain in price outweighs the percentage loss in units, so total revenue rises. Necessities are a classic inelastic example because buyers have few alternatives.
questions.hint: Small quantity response means inelastic demand and a revenue gain from higher price.

questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: Corrigan Analytics, a startup firm sets the price of a new Cloverdale service by estimating what customers believe it is worth, then working backward to the costs it can afford to incur. Which pricing approach is this?
questions.explanation: Value-based pricing starts with the customer's perceived worth and works backward to costs, so the price captures the value delivered. Cost-plus pricing instead adds a markup to costs, and competition-based pricing anchors on rivals' prices. Penetration pricing is a low initial price to win share, which is a different decision.
questions.hint: Ask what the price is anchored to: customer worth or company cost.

options.misconception: confuses a value estimate with a low launch price
assumes price is set by adding a margin to cost
mistakes customer worth for rivals' prices

questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: Yarrow HomeGoods, a startup firm sells two Linden items separately for $67 and $32. A bundle priced 28 percent below the sum of the separate prices would cost how much?
questions.explanation: The separate prices add to $99. A 28 percent discount removes $28, leaving a bundle price of $71. Adding without discounting ignores the promotion, quoting the discount reports the saving rather than the price, and applying the discount twice would overstate the reduction. Bundling works when buyers value the combination.
questions.hint: Add the two prices, then subtract the stated percentage of that sum.
